title: Al-Falaq: the daybreak
hook: refuge with the Lord of the dawn from darkness, knots and envy (Surah 113)

segments.voice: Yesterday: An-Nas, the last surah, and the whisperer who draws back when Allah is remembered. Your line was the whisperer withdraws. Did you catch a whisper, and did it back off? Day one hundred sixty.

If you've ever been awake before dawn, you know the moment. For a long time it's simply dark. Then a thin gray line opens along the horizon, like a seam splitting, and the night that felt endless turns out to have an edge. Yesterday's surah was about the danger inside, the whisper. Its twin, the surah just before it, is about dangers from outside: the dark, harm done in secret, other people's envy. And it names the One it turns to in a striking way. Not the Lord of the night. The Lord of the break. Today: Al-Falaq, the daybreak.
screen: `A GRAY LINE ON THE HORIZON.` → `THE NIGHT HAS AN EDGE.` → `THE LORD OF THE BREAK.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred thirteen opens, in Pickthall's translation: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak. Falaq comes from a root meaning to split. The same root describes a seed splitting open to sprout, and the dawn splitting the dark. So the first thing the surah tells you about the One you run to is that He is the one who breaks the night open. Then it names four things to seek refuge from. First, the evil in what He created: a general line, covering anything that can go wrong in a created world. Second, the darkness when it settles in, the night, and everything that feels bigger in it. Third, those who blow on knots. Commentators explain this as sorcery, the practice of tying knots and breathing spells on them. Muslims hold that such harm is real and that Allah's protection is greater. Fourth, the envier when he envies. Envy here isn't just wanting what someone has; it's wanting them not to have it. The surah doesn't ask you to fight any of these yourself. It asks you to say: I seek refuge. An-Nas and Al-Falaq are called together al-mu'awwidhatan, the two refuge surahs. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ recited them often, and a hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says that reciting them with al-Ikhlas three times in the morning and three in the evening is enough protection for everything. So yesterday's surah was for the night. This one fits the morning, the first light, when the day and whatever it brings are about to begin.
screen: `FALAQ — TO SPLIT, LIKE A SEED OR DAWN.` · `FOUR THINGS TO SEEK REFUGE FROM.` · `ENVY — WANTING THEM NOT TO HAVE IT.` · `THE TWO REFUGE SURAHS.` · then, large: `LORD OF THE DAYBREAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, for now and for tomorrow morning. Sit, and picture the first gray light of a dawn you've seen. Hold it. Now think of one thing about the day ahead that feels like the dark: a meeting, a worry, a person who wishes you ill. Don't solve it. Just set it in front of the light. If you pray, you can say the first line: qul a'udhu bi rabbil-falaq. Tomorrow, try it at first light. The bell holds the time.
Al-Falaq. The daybreak, from a root meaning to split open, the name of Surah one hundred thirteen. Today's word.
Your line: lord of the daybreak. When something today feels like it will never end, remember that the night has an edge. Look for the first gray line. Day one hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite al-Falaq with an-Nas and al-Ikhlas three times in the morning and three times in the evening, after the prayers, and before sleep, as the Prophet recommended.

original.note: Arabic: the daybreak, from f-l-q, to split, as a seed splits or dawn breaks the dark.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about the morning.
what it means: refuge in the Lord who splits the dawn from harm in creation, the dark, sorcery and envy.
what a scholar hears: f-l-q also in 6:95, the splitter of grain and seed; with Surah 114, al-mu'awwidhatan, recited morning, evening and before sleep.

sources.quoted: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak

sources.ref: Qur'an 113:2–5 (created things, darkness, blowers on knots, the envier)
Qur'an 6:95 (the splitter of grain and date-stone, same root)
Sunan Abi Dawud 5082; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3575 (three times morning and evening)

notes: Please confirm the exact Pickthall wording of 113:1.

Sorcery: the script says Muslims hold such harm is real and Allah's protection greater; some modern Muslims read 'blowers on knots' more figuratively (e.g. those who sow discord). Keeper may wish to add that.
Surah 113 is placed before 114 in the mushaf; the script calls it 'the surah just before it'.
